issues.legal_issue: The balance of convenience must be considered when deciding whether to grant an interim injunction against the collection of disputed property tax.
material_facts: The application sought an interim injunction restraining collection of house tax while a suit challenging the assessment was pending.
The house had never been let to a tenant, and the assessment was disputed.
The tax revenue supported the public body's civic services.
The lower appellate court found that any excess tax could be refunded or adjusted and that refusal of an injunction would not cause irreparable injury.
issues.conclusion: The balance of convenience could not be ignored; the refusal of the interim injunction was restored.
issues.legal_principle: An interim injunction is discretionary equitable relief, and the balance of convenience is a relevant consideration. The Court held that the High Court erred in treating that consideration as inapplicable where a prima facie case of erroneous assessment was shown.

predicates.tax_collection_injunction_application: A party applies for an interim injunction against collection of disputed tax while a challenge to the tax assessment is pending.
predicates.tax_revenue_funds_public_services: The public body relies on tax revenue to provide civic or other public services.
predicates.excess_tax_can_be_refunded_or_adjusted: If the tax is later found to have been overpaid, the excess can be refunded or credited against future tax.

issues.definition: When an interim injunction application concerns tax collection, the tax funds public services, and excess payment can be refunded or adjusted, the balance of convenience must be considered.

issues.legal_issue: The availability of an ordinary appeal against a tax assessment is relevant to whether a prima facie case for interim injunctive relief exists, but does not by itself decide whether the suit is barred.
material_facts: An ordinary appeal against the assessment was available to the assessee.
There was no finding that the assessee was unable to deposit the required amount before appealing.
The Court expressly declined to decide whether the suit was barred on that ground.
issues.conclusion: The available appeal and the absence of a finding that the assessee could not make the required deposit were relevant to whether a prima facie case existed for an interim injunction; the Court left the question whether the suit was barred undecided.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41(h) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 provides that an injunction is not to be granted where an equally efficacious relief is obtainable in another usual mode or proceeding, subject to the stated exception for breach of trust. The availability of an ordinary appeal therefore bears on the prima facie case for an interim injunction, though the Court did not decide that the suit was barred.

predicates.tax_assessment_injunction_application: A party applies for an interim injunction in a suit challenging a tax assessment.
predicates.ordinary_appeal_available: An ordinary appeal against the assessment is available to the assessee.
predicates.no_inability_to_make_required_deposit_fo: The court has made no finding that the assessee is unable to make a deposit required to pursue the appeal.

issues.definition: In a tax-assessment injunction application, when an ordinary appeal is available and inability to make its required deposit has not been found, the alternative remedy is relevant to whether a prima facie case exists.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court errs by interfering with concurrent refusals of an interim injunction on the basis of a misapprehension of the assessment law.
material_facts: The trial court and the appellate court both refused an interim injunction after finding that no prima facie case had been made out.
The High Court interfered in revision after relying on an assessment principle it considered applicable to premises that had never been let.
The Supreme Court held that the High Court had itself misapprehended the law and restored the appellate court's order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's revisional interference was set aside, and the appellate court's refusal of the interim injunction was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs revisional interference. The Court directed attention to the principles stated in Baldevdas Shivlal v. Filmistan Distributors (India) (P) Ltd., D.L.P. Housing and Construction Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. Samp Singh, and Managing Director (MIG), Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. Ajit Prasad Tarway, and held that the High Court had overlooked the governing limits on revision when it intervened on a misapprehension of the assessment law.

predicates.revision_from_interim_injunction_order: A party seeks revision of an order deciding an application for an interim injunction.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_refusal: The trial court and the appellate court have both refused the interim injunction.
predicates.high_court_interfered_on_misapprehended_: The High Court interferes because it considers the lower courts' decision to rest on an assessment-law principle that the Supreme Court finds misapprehended.

issues.definition: When revision concerns an interim injunction, both lower courts refused relief, and the High Court intervenes on a misapprehended assessment-law principle, revisional interference is unwarranted.
